newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain puts troops on alert for Zaire relief force.
newsitem.headline: Spain puts troops on alert for Zaire relief force.

text.p: Spain put troops on alert on Monday to go to Zaire and said a multinational force might be sent to open humanitarian corridors for refugees before the United Nations mounts its own relief effort.
Defence Minister Eduardo Serra said the U.N. Security Council was trying to mobilise its own military force to help the distribution of aid to more than a million refugeees.
"But there is a chance of sending before that a multinational force, and we are now making efforts for its organisation and dispatch, as quickly and as urgently as possible," Serra said.

On Saturday, the U.N. Security Council called on member states to lay the groundwork for a multinational force to help end the crisis in eastern Zaire but postponed its deployment until a later stage.

"Spain understands it is urgent to intervene," said Serra. "Spain has given urgent orders to make preparations and alert our troops in anticipation that it will be possible" to deploy them immediately, he added.
Spain has backed France in spearheading efforts to immediately send such a force to Zaire.
The U.N. Security Council on Saturday gave Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, a strong supporter of a multinational force, until November 20 to report on its framework and operations.

The council's failure to authorise immediate deployment enraged European Commissioner for humanitarian aid Emma Bonino, who accused the U.N. of not caring about the fate of thousands of refugees in Zaire.
Boutros-Ghali himself said on Sunday thousands were dying each hour.
In Addis Ababa, Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi hit out at the United Nations for calling on African nations to pay for their participation in any peace force for eastern Zaire.
The Spanish defence minister did not say how many soldiers would be in the planned force.

But last week, a Spanish foreign ministry spokesman said Spain and France wanted at least 5,000 soldiers, with 1,000 coming from France, fewer than 1,000 from Spain and the rest from the United States and other countries.
The eastern Zaire town of Kindu has been mentioned by Spanish officials as a possible destination for the force.

The United States, cool to the idea of a multinational force, said on Monday it had seen no coherent plans for one and did not know what the scope of the force would be or who was going to pay for it.
Britain has also said it is unlikely to send troops.

Meanwhile, Zaire and Rwanda have both agreed to allow humanitarian aid in. Foreign aid workers took some aid into the eastern Zairean city of Goma on Monday, but more than a million refugees remained beyond reach and were reported to be dying in their thousands.
The refugees have abandoned their camps in in eastern Zaire during the three-week-old conflict, where Tutsi rebels are fighting Zairean troops backed by Rwandan Hutu hardliners.
